---
title: "Precision"
description: "The fraction of predicted positive cases that are actually positive."
term: "Precision"
letter: "P"
category: "Model Evaluation"
difficulty: "Beginner"
---

## Simple explanation

Precision answers: “Of the cases the model flagged as positive, how many
really were positive?” It is important when false alarms are costly.

## Technical explanation

For a binary classifier, precision is
$\mathrm{TP}/(\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP})$, where TP is the number of true
positives and FP the number of false positives. If there are no predicted
positives, the denominator is zero and a metric library must apply an
explicitly chosen convention.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

In moderation, fraud review, or alerting, a high false-positive rate can
waste human effort or harm users. Precision should be considered alongside
recall and at the operating threshold that matches the use case.

## How it works

Choose a classification threshold, compare predictions with labeled
outcomes, and count true and false positives. Changing the threshold usually
changes both precision and recall, so teams examine a precision-recall curve
or select a threshold on validation data.

## Practical example

If a model flags 100 transactions and 80 are confirmed fraudulent, its
precision is $80/100=0.8$, or 80%. This does not reveal how many fraudulent
transactions the model missed; that is measured by recall.

## Common misconceptions

- Precision is not the same as overall accuracy.
- A high-precision model may have low recall if it flags only a small number
  of very clear positives.
